en: The Sūtra on the Saṃsāra of the Six Destinies,
Compiled by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven during the Chao-san Dafu [era].
I take refuge in the Honored One of the three times, who spoke of the Perfectly Awakened One’s teachings;
he constantly practices for the benefit of others and accumulates all manner of merit.
Whatever deeds of body, speech, or mind—whether good or evil—I have committed, [I confess them all].
The ripening of karmic fruits is certainly never in error, And there is no other creator.
The Supreme Guide, having realized this through direct perception,
Bestows compassion upon all sentient beings, And teaches that one receives retribution according to one's karma.
This accords with correct principle; having heard it, you should receive it with understanding.
All actions are of one's own mind, which, acting as the cause, causes one to race through the six realms of existence.
Out of fear of the three poisons, one traffics in the lives of all beings.
Having nurtured [a being] and then killed another, one shall fall into the Reviving Hell; there,
for a lifespan of a hundred thousand years, one is struck with knives,
staves, and clubs, and though dead, is born again to undergo such retribution of suffering.
Toward one's parents and kinsmen, one conceives harmful intent;
by uttering false speech and practicing deception, one shall fall into the Black Thread Hell.
A black thread is drawn across one’s body, just as wood is split in the world.
The saw blazes with fierce flames, and one suffers such retribution for their suffering.
If one burns mountains and rivers, forests and plains with fire,
harming and injuring sentient beings, one shall fall into the Hell of Intense Heat.
Flames burn everywhere, and the cries of suffering never cease;
with no light in both eyes, one undergoes such retribution for suffering.
This is because one spoke of what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma, and slandered others without basis.
Causing others to give rise to burning affliction, they fall into the Hell of Extreme Heat;
these sinful beings, oppressed by great fires,
are scorched without a moment's rest, receiving such retribution for their suffering.
Those who kill pigs, sheep, foxes, rabbits,
and other such living beings in infinite numbers shall fall into the Saṃghāta Hell;
having been born in that hell, they will undergo all manner of agonizing torments.
Tortured until death and then reborn again, they undergo such retribution for their suffering.
Having given rise to evil in body, speech, and mind, and having slandered and sowed discord among others—
such sinful beings shall fall into the Raurava Hell.
Those blazing and fierce flames burn without ceasing;
constantly emitting great, evil cries, they undergo such retribution for their suffering.
If one [acts thus] toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as toward those who are poor and destitute...
Having plundered and stolen the wealth of others, one falls into the Great Howling Hell;
scorched and roasted by fire, one undergoes the most extreme heat and affliction,
emitting loud, fierce, and evil cries as one receives such retribution for suffering.
Toward one's parents, teachers, elders, and virtuous sages,
if one gives rise to the intent to commit murder, one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell;
there, a mass of blazing, flaming fire will burn through and right to the very marrow of the bones.
For a long time they undergo extreme suffering, certain that there is not even a moment’s joy.
They give rise to enmity, hostility, and strife;
with spears and halberds they slaughter one another, and upon death they fall into the Copper-Clawed Hell, whose features are exceedingly sharp and keen.
They tear one another apart, or transform into knives and clubs,
vying with one another to hack and stab their bodies, thus receiving such bitter retribution.
Having used violence to invade the forms of others, they later fall into the Iron Spikes Hell.
Stakes sixteen finger-widths long pierce through the flesh and penetrate the bone;
furthermore, there are great iron women with flaming fangs most terrifying,
who devour from the crown of the head down to the heels, undergoing such retributive suffering.
If one plots with secret schemes to harm others, one will fall into that Forest of Sword-leaves,
where mad dogs, vultures, and eagles pursue and compete to devour [the victim].
If one plunders the wealth of others, one shall undergo extreme suffering.
Constantly swallowing hot iron balls, And further drenched with molten copper;
Having harmed sentient beings without cause, One shall fall into the Iron Hawk Hell,
Where sharp talons strike and peck, Causing suffering for a long duration.
If a person delights in wounding and killing the lives of aquatic creatures and other beings,
they will later fall into the River of Molten Copper, to be burned and boiled by the fires of their own karma.
If one, out of greed for one's own prosperity, suppresses and disparages the virtues of others, [they shall likewise suffer].
Falling into that Iron Grinding Hell, one wails in grief with no deliverance.
If a person does not act for the benefit of others, they shall undergo many forms of suffering:
two mountains shall press upon their body, afflicting it with further torment.
If one speaks what is not the Dharma and destroys the bridge,
they shall be driven along a path of sharp blades to come and go.
For wounding lice and fleas with armor, they shall fall into the mountain of Two-Goat-Head.
Striking one another, they die and are reborn again, transmigrating through cycles of suffering.
Relying on the path of liberation yet failing to guard the prohibitive precepts,
they fall into the Hell of Hot Ashes, where their limbs are entirely consumed and rotted away.
Feigning various dignified postures, they seek a livelihood through crooked means;
they fall into the Hell of Corpse Excrement, where they are devoured by maggots.
Seeing insects within the five grains, they do not choose them out but instead grind and thresh them all.
Falling into the Iron Mortar Hell, one is constantly pounded and crushed by them.
Those who rejoice at the suffering of others, who are deceitful and full of doubt,
and who always harbor a mind of anger and malice, become the henchmen of Yama.
The seeds of all bitter fruits have been briefly and concisely analyzed;
through the purification of body, speech, and mind, one shall ultimately and forever remain far removed from them.
The section on the hell realms concludes.
If a person takes no delight in giving, And further steals the food and drink of others,
They will fall among the *mahāgalagaṇḍa* ghosts, Constantly devouring various kinds of filth and excrement.
If one obstructs another from practicing generosity, Or gives rise to stinginess regarding their own possessions, [they shall likewise suffer].
One falls among the *sūcīmukha* ghosts, with a vast belly yet perpetually hungry and thirsty.
One who has no heirs and is stingy with wealth, neither giving it away nor enjoying it oneself,
falls among the *vañjula* ghosts, receiving only the leavings discarded by others.
Hoping for others' generosity, yet feeling regret for one's own meager giving,
one falls among the inferior pretas, constantly eating saliva and vomit.
Delighting in hearing the faults of others, one spreads them abroad with harsh words.
They fall among the *Yamamukha* pretas, enduring all manner of suffering for a long time.
Those who delight in inciting strife and possess not even a slight heart of compassion fall among the *Pariplava* pretas, where they eat wriggling insects and the like.
If one uses intimidation to seize the wealth of others, and having obtained it, gives but little in charity,
one will fall among the most hideous ghosts, receiving meager offerings while others are terrified.
If many people indulge in feasting and pleasure, slaughtering the lives of numerous creatures on a vast scale—
If one eats for oneself and gives to others, one will later fall among the rākṣasa demons.
If, regarding offerings of incense and flowers, one either sniffs them or takes them privately out of a slight heart of greed, one will later become a gandharva demon.
If one receives the veneration of others, yet harbors expectations for gain from them,
displaying an angry countenance while coveting their wealth, they will later become a fierce and evil ghost. If one marries another person,
yet constantly delights in acting as a matchmaker or mediator, [they will likewise fall into such states].
Later, harboring malice, they depart; upon death, they become *pūtana* ghosts.
If a person delights in drinking alcohol, exceeding moderation and becoming intoxicated and disorderly, or if they encourage others to do so, they will later become a *yakṣa* ghost.
Those who oppose the wishes of their parents, teachers,
and elders will later be born in the realm of yakṣas, fierce, powerful, and full of violence.
Due to the fault of stinginess and greed, they are constantly reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta).
Suffering and pleasure follow their own causes; therefore, do not create them again.
[The section on] the realm of hungry ghosts ends.
Regarding humans, devas, and the three evil realms, one can only rescue oneself.
Racing through the six realms of existence, like a dream-scene coming together;
beholding one's own and others' kin, one laments that they will not last long—
just like those actors who repeatedly change their appearances.
Having finished undergoing the sufferings of hell, one may be born among the devas;
when merit is exhausted, one sinks again and falls into the realm of animals.
Having assumed various forms and colors, one later attains birth in the human world.
Poverty and suffering are most arduous, like the revolving of a wheel;
this concludes the realm of animals.
As for the lifespan in the human realm, its measure is originally long and far-reaching.
Having frequently created the causes for killing, one thereby suffers diminution.
Enveloped by the sufferings of various diseases— such as leprosy, emaciation, and pestilence—
one is possessed by malevolent spirits and subjected to the beatings of royal law.
If a person, in pursuit of wealth and profit, exerts great labor and makes vast aspirations,
yet lacks even a slight intention to give in charity, they will later become a *dhana-pālaka* ghost who guards hoarded wealth.
If a person steals another's property and uses it, or perhaps even gives it away, [they shall suffer the same fate].
Later, having fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts, one loses whatever is obtained as soon as it is acquired.
If a person gives away their own wealth according to their means,
they shall obtain abundance and shall not be harmed or plundered by others.
If a person uses pure wealth to practice extensive giving while free from stinginess,
they will obtain exquisite food and drink, and all their desires will be fulfilled as they wish.
If a person offers precious delicacies with a pure mind, [they shall likewise receive such rewards].
The meritorious rewards one thereby obtains are physical beauty, strength, longevity, and peace.
If a person gives clothing as an offering, they will give rise to joy and delight;
they will attain a dignified and handsome appearance and be endowed with the robes of shame and modesty.
If one constructs a monastery for the Sangha and joyfully offers it as a gift,
they will experience the splendor of celestial palaces, replete with all five sensory pleasures.
If one builds bridges and provides gifts such as carriages and vehicles, [the same merit shall be attained].
One attains the highest peace and security, and a carriage of precious jewels.
If a person, in the midst of a wilderness, provides ponds, wells, springs,
and flowing streams, then wherever they are born, they shall never suffer from thirst or the torment of heat.
If a person gives away a favorite concubine, adorned and beautifully arrayed,
the fruit and retribution they obtain will be the fulfillment of sensual pleasures, wealth, and nobility.
If a person gives away the sutras and teachings, as well as secular literary works, [the merit is likewise vast].
One who is able to maintain [these virtues] and bestow them upon others will experience the fruit of extensive learning and great wisdom.
If a person gives medicine, as well as the gift of fearlessness,
the retribution they obtain will be peace and happiness, free from terror.
If one gives lamps, one’s eyes will always be pure;
If one gives music, one will obtain exquisite sounds;
If one gives bedding and seats, one will attain peace and happiness.
If one gives servants, one will be constantly surrounded by attendants;
by giving milch cows and such things, one obtains beauty, strength, and longevity;
if one gives fertile fields, one obtains overflowing storehouses and granaries.
To each and every seeker, according to their respective desires,
he provides flowers, fruits, and clear springs, consoling them with loving speech.
Furthermore, there are those who, though practicing giving, employ others for labor while bestowing little themselves.
If one gives out of fear, or out of a desire for praise from others;
or seeks present wealth and status, or rebirth in heaven to enjoy happiness—
such acts of giving yield extremely meager merit.
If one delights in practicing altruism, Not begrudging even body or life,
And always harbors a heart of compassion, The fruit of sainthood is not difficult to attain.
To all who come as supplicants, One should give according to the proper time.
Causing them to give rise to joy and satisfaction, they will experience results according to their wishes.
If one gives to others with difficulty, the time of receiving the retribution will be likewise;
to withhold from oneself and bestow upon others is the supreme dharma of peace and happiness.
Generosity is the root of all happiness, just as planting seeds produces their fruit;
out of compassion for those who come seeking, give according to their needs so they do not return empty-handed.
Be careful never to covet the forms of others; look upon them as you would your own children.
Even toward one's own wife, one should immediately cease any arising desire.
If a person binds their mind to objects of sensual pleasure and clings to them with delight,
they will be reborn in the world hereafter and certainly receive the retribution of a female body.
If a person grows weary of the female body, renounces desire, upholds the pure precepts,
and gives rise to a firm resolve, they will transform their rebirth into that of a man.
If a person cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they shall be free from all harm and affliction.
Possessing merit, virtue, and majestic power, they are constantly revered by devas and humans.
If a person does not drink alcohol, abides in right mindfulness,
and always speaks words of truth, they will obtain peace and security in the present life.
If one sees others in discord, one should exhort and persuade them to be harmonious;
thus one will experience a vast retinue and be free from the suffering of separation.
Regarding the instructions of teachers and elders, one should always listen and receive them with joy.
One who weighs gain and loss with further deliberation possesses skillful wisdom.
Those who are impoverished and serve as laborers often delight in inflicting beatings;
though they have committed no fault, they distress others, adding further suffering to their own misery.
If a person possesses a handsome form and, relying upon it, gives rise to pride and mocks others,
they shall receive the retribution of being short and hunchbacked.
If a person is by nature stingy and base, and feigns not hearing when others try to guide them well, [they shall suffer likewise].
Those who are extremely heavy in their ignorance shall receive the retribution of deafness and muteness.
Performing good deeds brings further blessings; accumulating evil invites suffering and affliction.
Each brings about its own cause, and according to one's karma, one must inevitably experience the result.
The retribution for the human realm is concluded.
Constantly practicing deceit and hypocrisy, delighting in anger, resentment, and strife,
yet by virtue of having practiced generosity in the past, one becomes a lord of the asuras.
The section on the realm of asuras concludes.
Those who joyfully cultivate the causes of the ten wholesome deeds and refrain from harming others are constantly protected by the devas and shall be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
By showing reverence to one's parents and the Triple Gem, giving according to one's ability,
and possessing patience and gentleness, one will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
By not delighting in anger or strife oneself and encouraging others to be harmonious and compliant, one attains this state.
By purely cultivating wholesome causes, one is born in the Yāma Heaven.
Delighting in hearing the True Dharma and single-mindedly practicing the wisdom of liberation,
and joyfully praising the merits of others, one is born in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Regarding the practices of generosity and ethical discipline, they always delight in their essential nature;
by giving rise to diligent and heroic effort, they are born in the Heaven of Emanation.
These are the most supreme of sentient beings, fully possessing the ascetic life of a śramaṇa.
Increasing the causes for liberation, one attains birth in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
Through the cultivation of precepts and meditative concentration, universally supported by the power of vows,
one is born among gods and humans, reaching the reality-limit of True Suchness.
Thus have the retributions of good and evil been clearly demonstrated:
practicing good invites rebirth among gods and humans; committing evil entangles one in extreme suffering.
Before old age, illness, and death arrive, diligently contemplate and seek the True Dharma.
Since the retribution of one's own karma has already brought about the separation from all that is beloved, those faults such as craving should be viewed with deep revulsion.
The wise reflect well upon this; therefore, they should distance themselves from them.
If one constantly practices benefiting others, Then there will be no obstacles or afflictions;
The distinction between sin and merit is certain— Listen attentively to this brief explanation.
*Sūtra on the Cycle of the Six Realms*
